claim: The anatomically defined compartments of the insect mushroom body function as parallel units of associative learning, with different learning rates, memory decay dynamics and flexibility.
source: The anatomically defined compartments of the insect mushroom body function as parallel units of associative learning, with different learning rates, memory decay dynamics and flexibility (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claim: Nitric oxide (NO) acts as a neurotransmitter in a subset of dopaminergic neurons in Drosophila.
source: Here, we show that nitric oxide (NO) acts as a neurotransmitter in a subset of dopaminergic neurons in Drosophila.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including RNA-seq, immunohistochemistry, and behavioral experiments.

claim: NO's effects develop more slowly than those of dopamine.
source: NO's effects develop more slowly than those of dopamine and depend on soluble guanylate cyclase in postsynaptic Kenyon cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing slower memory formation kinetics with NO compared to dopamine (Figure 6).

claim: NO's effects depend on soluble guanylate cyclase in postsynaptic Kenyon cells.
source: NO's effects develop more slowly than those of dopamine and depend on soluble guanylate cyclase in postsynaptic Kenyon cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNAi knockdown experiments showing that Gycβ100B in Kenyon cells is required for NO-dependent memory (Figure 5C).

claim: NO acts antagonistically to dopamine.
source: NO acts antagonistically to dopamine; it shortens memory retention and facilitates the rapid updating of memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing opposite valence memories in TH mutants (Figure 1, Figure 2) and by memory retention experiments (Figure 6D).

claim: NO shortens memory retention.
source: NO acts antagonistically to dopamine; it shortens memory retention and facilitates the rapid updating of memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that NOS-RNAi or L-NNA feeding prolongs memory retention (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: NO facilitates the rapid updating of memories.
source: NO acts antagonistically to dopamine; it shortens memory retention and facilitates the rapid updating of memories.
evidence: This claim is supported by reversal learning experiments showing faster memory updating in wild-type flies compared to L-NNA fed or TH mutant flies (Figure 7B).

claim: The interplay of NO and dopamine enables memories stored in local domains along Kenyon cell axons to be specialized for predicting the value of odors based only on recent events.
source: The interplay of NO and dopamine enables memories stored in local domains along Kenyon cell axons to be specialized for predicting the value of odors based only on recent events.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral experiments showing rapid memory updating and modeling results (Figure 7, Figure 8).

claim: Multiple distributed neuronal circuits in the mammalian brain have been shown to process and store distinct facets of information acquired during learning.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that multiple distributed neuronal circuits in the mammalian brain have been shown to process and store distinct facets of information acquired during learning (White and McDonald, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to White and McDonald, 2002.

claim: Fear conditioning induces enduring changes, referred to as memory engrams, in circuits distributed across different brain areas.
source: Even a simple form of associative learning such as fear conditioning induces enduring changes, referred to as memory engrams, in circuits distributed across different brain areas (Herry and Johansen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herry and Johansen, 2014.

claim: Olfactory memory formation and retrieval in insects requires the MB.
source: Olfactory memory formation and retrieval in insects requires the MB (de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Dubnau et al., 2001; Erber et al., 1980; Heisenberg, 2003; McGuire et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In associative olfactory learning, exposure to an odor paired with a reward or punishment results in formation of a positive- or negative-valence memory, respectively.
source: In associative olfactory learning, exposure to an odor paired with a reward or punishment results in formation of a positive- or negative-valence memory, respectively (Quinn et al., 1974; Tempel et al., 1983; Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Quinn et al., 1974; Tempel et al., 1983; Tully and Quinn, 1985.

claim: In the MB, sensory stimuli are represented by the sparse activity of ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs).
source: In the MB, sensory stimuli are represented by the sparse activity of ~2000 Kenyon cells (KCs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila mushroom body.

claim: Each of 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) innervates compartmental regions along the parallel axonal fibers of the KCs.
source: Each of 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs) innervates compartmental regions along the parallel axonal fibers of the KCs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila mushroom body, supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014a; Mao and Davis, 2009; Tanaka et al., 2008.

claim: 22 types of mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) arborize their dendrites in specific axonal segments of the KCs.
source: Similarly, 22 types of mushroom body output neurons (MBONs) arborize their dendrites in specific axonal segments of the KCs; together, the arbors of the DANs and MBONs define the compartmental units of the MB (Aso et al., 2014a; Mao and Davis, 2009; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila mushroom body, supported by citations.

claim: Activation of individual MBONs can cause behavioral attraction or repulsion, depending on the compartment in which their dendrites arborize.
source: Activation of individual MBONs can cause behavioral attraction or repulsion, depending on the compartment in which their dendrites arborize, and MBONs appear to use a population code to govern behavior (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b; Owald et al., 2015.

claim: MBONs appear to use a population code to govern behavior.
source: Activation of individual MBONs can cause behavioral attraction or repulsion, depending on the compartment in which their dendrites arborize, and MBONs appear to use a population code to govern behavior (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso et al., 2014b; Owald et al., 2015.

claim: The anatomically defined compartments of the MB are the units of associative learning.
source: A large body of evidence indicates that these anatomically defined compartments of the MB are also the units of associative learning (Aso et al., 2012; Aso et al., 2014b; Aso et al., 2010; Berry et al., 2018; Blum et al., 2009; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2012; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Isabel et al., 2004; Krashes et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2012; Owald et al., 2015; Pai et al., 2013; Plaçais et al., 2013; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Séjourné et al., 2011; Trannoy et al., 2011; Yamagata et al., 2015; Zars et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations.

claim: Dopaminergic neurons and signaling play a key role in all MB compartments.
source: Nevertheless, dopaminergic neurons and signaling play a key role in all MB compartments, and flies can be trained to form associative memories by pairing the presentation of an odor with stimulation of a single dopaminergic neuron (Aso et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso et al., 2010.

claim: Flies can be trained to form associative memories by pairing the presentation of an odor with stimulation of a single dopaminergic neuron.
source: Nevertheless, dopaminergic neurons and signaling play a key role in all MB compartments, and flies can be trained to form associative memories by pairing the presentation of an odor with stimulation of a single dopaminergic neuron (Aso et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso et al., 2010.

claim: Punishment or reward activates distinct sets of DANs that innervate specific compartments of the MB.
source: Punishment or reward activates distinct sets of DANs that innervate specific compartments of the MB (Das et al., 2014; Galili et al., 2014; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Liu et al., 2012; Mao and Davis, 2009; Riemensperger et al., 2005; Tomchik, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Activation of the DAN innervating an MB compartment induces enduring depression of KC-MBONs synapses in those specific KCs that were active in that compartment at the time of dopamine release.
source: Activation of the DAN innervating an MB compartment induces enduring depression of KC-MBONs synapses in those specific KCs that were active in that compartment at the time of dopamine release (Berry et al., 2018; Bouzaiane et al., 2015; Cohn et al., 2015; Hige et al., 2015; Owald et al., 2015; Séjourné et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Which compartment receives dopamine during training determines the valence of the memory.
source: Thus, which compartment receives dopamine during training appears to determine the valence of the memory, while which KCs were active during training determines the sensory specificity of the memory (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Which KCs were active during training determines the sensory specificity of the memory.
source: Thus, which compartment receives dopamine during training appears to determine the valence of the memory, while which KCs were active during training determines the sensory specificity of the memory (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In wild-type flies, PPL1 cluster DAN activation paired with odor induces robust negative-valence memory.
source: In flies with a wild-type TH allele, this training protocol induced robust negative-valence memory of the paired odor (Figure 1D), as observed previously (Claridge-Chang et al., 2009; Schroll et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citations to previous studies.

claim: In the dopamine-deficient background, activation of PPL1 DANs induces a robust odor memory with positive valence.
source: In the dopamine-deficient background, activation of the same DANs still induced a robust odor memory, but its valence was now positive (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TH mutant flies show a weak positive-valence memory after odor-shock conditioning.
source: This result is consistent with previous findings that TH mutant flies show a weak positive-valence memory after odor-shock conditioning (Riemensperger et al., 2011), although the positive-valence memory we observed is much stronger.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riemensperger et al., 2011.

claim: Feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa to adult-stage flies fully restored normal valence memory.
source: Arguing against the possibility that this valence-inversion phenotype resulted from a developmental defect caused by the constitutive absence of dopamine (Niens et al., 2017), feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa to adult-stage flies fully restored normal valence memory (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Restoring TH expression specifically in the PPL1 DANs was sufficient to restore formation of negative-valence memory.
source: Nor did the valence-inversion phenotype result from lack of dopamine signaling outside the MB, as restoring TH expression specifically in the PPL1 DANs was sufficient to restore formation of negative-valence memory (Figure 1G; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of reward-representing PAM cluster DANs in the TH mutant background induces odor memory of negative valence.
source: Moreover, valence-inversion in the absence of dopamine was not limited to punishment-representing DANs. Activation of reward-representing PAM cluster DANs (Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012) in the TH mutant background also induced odor memory of opposite valence, in this case negative rather than positive (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D,E and citations to Burke et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012.

claim: Either L-DOPA plus carbidopa feeding or TH expression in reward-representing DANs restored the ability to form a memory of the valence that is observed in wild-type flies.
source: as we found for PPL1-induced memories, either L-DOPA plus carbidopa feeding or TH expression in reward-representing DANs restored the ability to form a memory of the valence that is observed in wild-type flies (Figure 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F,G.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc stimulation in TH mutant animals switches memory valence from negative to positive.
source: We identified two DAN cell types that exhibited the valence-inversion phenotype: PPL1-γ1pedc and PAM-γ5/PAM-β'2a. With PPL1-γ1pedc stimulation, memory valence switched from negative to positive in TH mutant animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: With PAM-γ5 and PAM-β'2a stimulation, memory valence flipped from positive to negative in TH mutants.
source: Conversely, with PAM-γ5 and PAM-β'2a stimulation, memory valence flipped in the opposite direction, from positive to negative in TH mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Activation of PPL1-γ2α'1 resulted in negative-valence memory in both TH mutant and wild type, suggesting a cotransmitter with the same sign of action as dopamine.
source: Activation of PPL1-γ2α'1 resulted in negative-valence memory in both TH mutant and wild type, suggesting a cotransmitter with the same sign of action as dopamine.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Activation of PPL1-α3 or PAM-β'1 in the TH mutant background did not induce significant memory, indicating that these cells do not express a cotransmitter capable of inducing memory without dopamine.
source: Activation of PPL1-α3 or PAM-β'1 in the TH mutant background did not induce significant memory, indicating that these cells do not express a cotransmitter capable of inducing memory without dopamine.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and represents an inference from the data.

claim: NOS1 was the most abundantly expressed isoform of nitric oxide synthase in the profiled DAN cell types.
source: NOS1 was the most abundantly expressed isoform as judged by RNA profiling.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only NOS1, the full-length isoform of Drosophila NOS, is functional.
source: Only NOS1, the full-length isoform, is functional, while the truncated isoforms can function as a dominant-negative.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stasiv et al., 2001.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc was labeled with FISH probes against NOS1 or NOS4 transcripts.
source: PPL1-γ1pedc was labeled with these FISH probes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), confirming expression of NOS1 or NOS4 in these cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In the MB lobes, the γ1pedc and γ5 compartments showed enriched anti-NOS immunoreactivity.
source: In the MB lobes, the γ1pedc and γ5 compartments showed enriched anti-NOS immunoreactivity, as expected from the RNA-Seq data (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NOS colocalizes with γ1pedc's terminals.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed colocalization of NOS with γ1pedc's terminals by expansion microscopy and lattice light sheet microscopy (ExM LLSM; Figure 3F and G, Video 1) (Chen et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2019; Tillberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by ExM LLSM data shown in Figure 3F and G, Video 1.

claim: Feeding flies the competitive NOS inhibitor L-NNA reduced valence-inverted memory formation in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that this treatment reduced valence-inverted memory formation in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When dopamine levels were restored by feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa, L-NNA fed flies showed a normal level of negative-valence odor memory formation in response to pairing an odor with PPL1-γ1pedc activation.
source: First, when we bypassed the TH mutant by feeding L-DOPA and carbidopa to restore dopamine levels, the L-NNA fed flies showed a normal level of negative-valence odor memory formation in response to pairing an odor with PPL1- γ1pedc activation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The effect of L-NNA feeding was cell-type specific; memory formed by activation of either PPL1-γ1pedc or PAM-γ5/β'2a was affected but that formed by activation of PPL1-γ2α'1, was not.
source: Second, the effect of L-NNA feeding was cell-type specific; memory formed by activation of either PPL1-γ1pedc or PAM-γ5/β'2a was affected but that formed by activation of PPL1-γ2α'1, was not (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expressing NOS-RNAi in all PPL1 DANs resulted in negative-valence memory in the TH mutant background.
source: We obtained consistent results in knockdown experiments where we expressed NOS-RNAi in all PPL1 DANs (Figure 4C). In this case, the negative-valence memory observed with NOS-RNAi in the TH mutant background is consistent with the presence of a different cotransmitter in PPL1-γ2α'1 (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When NOS was ectopically expressed in PPL1-α3, the same training protocol induced a positive-valence memory in TH mutant flies.
source: TH mutant flies formed no odor association with PPL1-α3 activation, but when NOS was ectopically expressed in the α3 compartment, the same training protocol induced a positive-valence memory (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Ectopic expression of NOS in PPL1-γ2α'1 resulted in valence inversion phenotype.
source: Similarly, ectopic expression of NOS in PPL1-γ2α'1 also resulted in valence inversion phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NO was able to form an association of opposite valence to that formed by dopamine.
source: In other words, NO was able to form an association of opposite valence to that formed by dopamine.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the ectopic expression experiments shown in Figure 4D, E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA-seq data revealed expression of the subunits of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), Gycα99B and Gycβ100B, in KCs, DANs, and MBONs.
source: RNA-seq data revealed expression of the subunits of soluble guanylate cyclase (sGC), Gycα99B and Gycβ100B, in KCs, DANs, and MBONs (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A–B.

claim: Drosophila sGC is activated upon binding NO.
source: Similar to its mammalian homologs, Drosophila sGC is activated upon binding NO (Morton et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Morton et al., 2005.

claim: A protein trap Gycβ100B-EGFP fusion protein was broadly expressed in the MB lobes.
source: Consistent with these transcriptomic data, we observed that a protein trap Gycβ100B-EGFP fusion protein (MI08892; Venken et al., 2011) was broadly expressed in the MB lobes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Venken et al., 2011.

claim: RNAi knockdown of Gycβ100B in KCs abolished the valence-inverted memory induced by activation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH mutant background.
source: We found that a reduction in Gycβ100B produced in this way abolished the valence-inverted memory induced by activation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH mutant background (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Flies carrying MB-switch driven Gycβ100B-RNAi do not have a general defect in learning.
source: Although MB-switch showed significant leaky expression without RU-486 feeding under our experimental conditions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F), we could restore normal aversive memory by feeding TH mutant flies L-DOPA (Figure 5C), indicating that flies carrying MB-switch driven Gycβ100B-RNAi do not have a general defect in learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: NO functions as cotransmitter that is released by DANs and acts on sGC in postsynaptic KCs to regulate cGMP levels.
source: Taken together, our data argue strongly that NO functions as cotransmitter that is released by DANs and acts on sGC in postsynaptic KCs to regulate cGMP levels, although our results do not exclude the possibility that NO has other targets.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data presented in Figures 3, 4, and 5.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background can induce a prolonged increase in calcium levels in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, which was suppressed by L-NNA.
source: Indeed, both MBONs and DANs express sGC (Figure 5B) and we found that optogenetic stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background can induce a prolonged increase in calcium levels in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, which was suppressed by L-NNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: DANs expressing sGC in other compartments did not respond to stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background.
source: However, DANs expressing sGC in other compartments did not respond to stimulation of PPL1-γ1pedc in a TH-mutant background (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B), raising the possibility that NO may not be able to diffuse over the 30 µm distances required to reach those compartments.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc induces a valence inverted memory when its activity precedes an odor such that the odor predicts relief from punishment.
source: PPL1-γ1pedc induces a valence inverted memory when its activity precedes an odor such that the odor predicts relief from punishment (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tanimoto et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Aso and Rubin, 2016; Tanimoto et al., 2004.

claim: NOS is dispensable for timing dependent inversion of memory valence.
source: NOS is dispensable for this timing dependent inversion of memory valence (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), an observation consistent with a recent report that timing dependent inversion of long-term-depression of KC-to-MBON synapses to long-term-potentiation is mediated by different dopamine receptors (Handler et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and a citation to Handler et al., 2019.

claim: RNAi knockdown of scrib impaired NO-dependent memory in TH-mutant flies.
source: RNAi knockdown of scrib impaired NO-dependent memory in TH-mutant flies (Figure 5D), suggesting a role of NO in regulating memory stability.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In wild-type flies, PPL1-γ1pedc activation as brief as 10 s can induce significant negative-valence memory.
source: In wild-type flies, PPL1-γ1pedc activation as brief as 10 s can induce significant negative-valence memory.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Blocking NOS activity with L-NNA did not affect the memory scores observed shortly after a wide range of training protocols.
source: Blocking NOS activity with L-NNA did not affect the memory scores observed shortly after a wide range of training protocols (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Longer and repetitive training was required to induce robust NO-dependent positive-valence memory in the absence of dopamine.
source: In contrast, longer and repetitive training was required to induce robust NO-dependent positive-valence memory in the absence of dopamine (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: NO-dependent memory develops slowly over time.
source: When we used a single cycle of training, we found that NO-dependent memory develops slowly over time. Memory scores were not significantly different from zero at 1, 3, 5 min after training, and only became significant after 10 min.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NO-dependent memories were long lasting and were still more than half maximal after 6 hr.
source: Once formed, however, these NO-dependent memories were long lasting and were still more than half maximal after 6 hr (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Expression of NOS-RNAi or L-NNA feeding prolonged the retention of memories induced by either optogenetic training with PPL1-γ1pedc or odor-shock conditioning.
source: Indeed, we found that expression of NOS-RNAi or L-NNA feeding prolonged the retention of memories induced by either optogenetic training with PPL1-γ1pedc or odor-shock conditioning (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: PPL1-γ1pedc fails to induce long-lasting memory even after 10x repetitive training at spaced intervals.
source: However, PPL1-γ1pedc fails to induce long-lasting memory even after 10x repetitive training at spaced intervals (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claim: Other DANs from the PPL1 cluster that do not exhibit significant NOS expression, PPL1-α3 or a combination of PPL1-γ2α'1 and PPL1-α'2α2, are able to induce stable memory lasting for 4 days after 10x spaced training.
source: In contrast, other DANs from the PPL1 cluster that do not exhibit significant NOS expression, PPL1-α3 or a combination of PPL1-γ2α'1 and PPL1-α'2α2, are able to induce stable memory lasting for 4 days after 10x spaced training (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claim: Spaced training with PPL1-γ1pedc induced memory lasting 1 day when NOS signaling was compromised, either by knockdown with RNAi or inhibition by L-NNA.
source: Spaced training with PPL1-γ1pedc induced memory lasting 1 day when NOS signaling was compromised, either by knockdown with RNAi (Figure 6E) or inhibition by L-NNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The valence-inverted memories formed in the γ1pedc compartment following repetitive training in TH mutants lasted 1 day after training.
source: The valence-inverted memories formed in the γ1pedc compartment following repetitive training in TH mutants also lasted 1 day after training (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: In wild-type flies, odor preference can be altered by a single trial of reversal conditioning with PPL1-γ1pedc activation.
source: In wild-type flies, odor preference can be altered by a single trial of reversal conditioning with PPL1-γ1pedc activation (Figure 7B, left)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B, left.

claim: When NOS was inhibited, switching odor preference required a repetition of reversal conditioning.
source: whereas this process became slower and required more training when NOS was inhibited (Figure 7B; center), such that switching odor preference required a repetition of reversal conditioning.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B; center.

claim: In TH mutants, NO-dependent memory was altered by reversal conditioning, but with an even slower time course.
source: In TH mutants, NO-dependent memory was also altered by reversal conditioning, but with an even slower time course (Figure 7B; right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B; right.

claim: Exposure to odors alone did not change the existing memory.
source: The second type of new experience, exposure to odors alone, did not change the existing memory in this assay (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: DAN activation alone quickly reduced conditioned odor response in wild-type flies.
source: The third type of new experience, DAN activation alone, quickly reduced conditioned odor response in wild-type flies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Inhibiting NOS slowed the reduction of conditioned odor response by DAN activation alone.
source: Inhibiting NOS slowed this process (Figure 7D; center).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D; center.

claim: NO-dependent memory was reduced by unpaired activation of DANs, but it took five trials to detect significant reduction.
source: NO-dependent memory was also reduced by unpaired activation of DANs, but it took five trials to detect significant reduction (Figure 7D; right).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D; right.

claim: Both the slow formation and the persistence of NO-dependent memory facilitate the fast updating of memories stored in NOS-positive MB compartments in response to changing conditions.
source: These results suggest that both the slow formation and the persistence of NO-dependent memory facilitate the fast updating of memories stored in NOS-positive MB compartments in response to changing conditions.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The multiplicative model provides a good match to the behavioral data.
source: We found that the multiplicative model provides a good match to our data (Figure 8C, blue curve).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Assuming that spontaneous activity in DANs leads to memory decay accounted for the NO-dependent reduction in memory lifetime.
source: Assuming that spontaneous activity in DANs leads to memory decay (Plaçais et al., 2012; Berry et al., 2018; Sitaraman et al., 2015) accounted for the NO-dependent reduction in memory lifetime that we observed (Figure 8E).
evidence: This claim is supported by modeling results shown in Figure 8E and citations to Plaçais et al., 2012; Berry et al., 2018; Sitaraman et al., 2015.

claim: The model cannot account for the enhanced persistence of memories after 10x training for DA or NO-null conditions, suggesting a recruitment of additional consolidation mechanisms after spaced conditioning.
source: A notable exception is that this model cannot account for the enhanced persistence of memories after 10x training for DA or NO-null conditions (Figure 6E), suggesting a recruitment of additional consolidation mechanisms after spaced conditioning, as previously proposed (Pagani et al., 2009; Tully et al., 1994; Pai et al., 2013; Scheunemann et al., 2018; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2013; Miyashita et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2012; Akalal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the modeling results and is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spaced training with PPL-α3 can induce long-lasting memory but it requires at least 3 hr after training to develop.
source: Also, we found that spaced training with PPL-α3 can induce long-lasting memory but it requires at least 3 hr after training to develop (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Protein synthesis in MBON-α3 in the first 3 hr time window after odor-shock spaced training is required for LTM formation.
source: This observation is consistent with the report that protein synthesis in MBON-α3 in the first 3 hr time window after odor-shock spaced training is required for LTM formation (Pai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pai et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Subsets of dopaminergic neurons co-release glutamate or GABA in rodents.
source: In rodents, subsets of dopaminergic neurons co-release glutamate or GABA (Maher and Westbrook, 2008; Stuber et al., 2010; Sulzer et al., 1998; Tecuapetla et al., 2010; Tritsch et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Single-cell expression profiling reveals expression of diverse neuropeptides in dopaminergic neurons in mice and Drosophila.
source: In mice and Drosophila, single-cell expression profiling reveals expression of diverse neuropeptides in dopaminergic neurons (Croset et al., 2018; Poulin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Croset et al., 2018; Poulin et al., 2014.

claim: EM connectome studies of the mushroom body in adult and larval Drosophila reveal the co-existence of small-clear-core and large-dense-core synaptic vesicles in individual terminals of dopaminergic neurons.
source: EM connectome studies of the mushroom body in adult and larval Drosophila reveal the co-existence of small-clear-core and large-dense-core synaptic vesicles in individual terminals of dopaminergic neurons (Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eichler et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017.

claim: The size of the observed large-dense-core vesicles differs between DAN cell types.
source: moreover, the size of the observed large-dense-core vesicles differs between DAN cell types (Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takemura et al., 2017.

claim: Drosophila NOS is regulated by Ca2+/calmodulin.
source: Drosophila NOS is regulated by Ca2+/calmodulin (Regulski and Tully, 1995), as is the neuronal isoform of NOS in the mammalian brain (Abu-Soud and Stuehr, 1993)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Regulski and Tully, 1995; Abu-Soud and Stuehr, 1993.

claim: The localization of the NOS1 protein in the axonal terminals of DANs is consistent with NO serving as a cotransmitter.
source: Furthermore, the localization of the NOS1 protein in the axonal terminals of DANs (Figure 3D) is consistent with NO serving as a cotransmitter.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: NO acts as a neurotransmitter in the Drosophila mushroom body, in contrast to a proposed cell-autonomous action of NOS in the ellipsoid body.
source: This role contrasts with the proposed cell-autonomous action of NOS in the ellipsoid body, in which NO appears to target proteins within the NOS-expressing ring neurons themselves, rather than conveying a signal to neighboring cells (Kuntz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data and is contrasted with a citation to Kuntz et al., 2017.

claim: The concentration of Ca2+ in KC axons represents olfactory information during olfactory learning.
source: During olfactory learning, the concentration of Ca2+ in KC axons represents olfactory information.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Drosophila mushroom body.

claim: The coincidence of a Ca2+ rise in spiking KCs and activation of the G-protein-coupled Dop1R1 dopamine receptor increases adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: The coincidence of a Ca2+ rise in spiking KCs and activation of the G-protein-coupled Dop1R1 dopamine receptor increases adenylyl cyclase activity (Abrams et al., 1998; Boto et al., 2014; Byrne et al., 1991; Kim et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2003; Tomchik and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The resultant cAMP activates protein kinase A.
source: The resultant cAMP in turn activates protein kinase A (Gervasi et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993), a signaling cascade that is important for synaptic plasticity and memory formation throughout the animal phyla (e.g. Davis et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gervasi et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993; Davis et al., 1995.

claim: When DANs are activated without KC activity, molecular pathways involving the Dop1R2 receptor, Rac1 and Scribble facilitate decay of memory.
source: In contrast, when DANs are activated without KC activity, and thus during low intracellular Ca2+ in the KCs, molecular pathways involving the Dop1R2 receptor, Rac1 and Scribble facilitate decay of memory (Berry et al., 2012; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2007; Shuai et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2012; Cervantes-Sandoval et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2007; Shuai et al., 2010.

claim: NO-dependent effect requires scribble in KCs, a gene previously reported as a component of active forgetting.
source: Indeed, NO-dependent effect requires scribble in KCs, a gene previously reported as a component of active forgetting (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D and references to previous work on scribble.

claim: In the vertebrate cerebellum, long-term-depression at parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses induced by climbing fibers can coexist with long-term-potentiation by NO.
source: In the vertebrate cerebellum, which has many architectural similarities to the MB (Farris, 2011; Marr, 1969; Medina et al., 2002), long-term-depression at parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses (equivalent to KC-MBON synapses) induced by climbing fibers (equivalent to DANs) can coexist with long-term-potentiation by NO (Bredt et al., 1990; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Shibuki and Okada, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The balance between LTD and LTP in the cerebellum was suggested to play an important role in preventing memory saturation and allowing reversal of motor learning.
source: In this case, the unaltered net synaptic weight results from a balance between coexisting LTD and LTP rather than recovery from LTD. This balance was suggested to play an important role in preventing memory saturation in the cerebellum and allowing reversal of motor learning.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited literature on the cerebellum.

claim: Opposing cotransmitters have been observed widely in both invertebrate and vertebrate neurons.
source: Opposing cotransmitters have been observed widely in both invertebrate and vertebrate neurons (Nusbaum et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nusbaum et al., 2017.

claim: A common feature of opposing cotransmitters is that the transmitters have distinct time courses of action.
source: A common feature in these cases is that the transmitters have distinct time courses of action.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the cited literature on opposing cotransmitters.

claim: Hypothalamic hypocretin-dynorphin neurons synthesize excitatory hypocretin and inhibitory dynorphin.
source: For instance, hypothalamic hypocretin-dynorphin neurons that are critical for sleep and arousal synthesize excitatory hypocretin and inhibitory dynorphin.
evidence: This is established knowledge about hypothalamic neurons.

claim: When hypocretin and dynorphin are released together repeatedly, the distinct kinetics of their receptors result in an initial outward current, then little current, and then an inward current in the postsynaptic cells.
source: When they are released together repeatedly, the distinct kinetics of their receptors result in an initial outward current, then little current, and then an inward current in the postsynaptic cells (Li and van den Pol, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li and van den Pol, 2006.

claim: Decades of behavioral genetic studies have identified more than one hundred genes underlying olfactory conditioning in Drosophila.
source: Decades of behavioral genetic studies have identified more than one hundred genes underlying olfactory conditioning in Drosophila (Keene and Waddell, 2007; McGuire et al., 2005; Thurmond et al., 2019; Walkinshaw et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutant and targeted rescue studies have been used to map the function of many memory-related genes to specific subsets of Kenyon cells.
source: Mutant and targeted rescue studies have been used to map the function of many memory-related genes encoding synaptic or intracellular signaling proteins (for example, rutabaga, DopR1/dumb, DopR2/DAMB, PKA-C1/DC0, Synapsin, Bruchpilot, Orb2 and Rac1) to specific subsets of Kenyon cells (Akalal et al., 2006; Berry et al., 2012; Blum et al., 2009; Gervasi et al., 2010; Han et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2007; Knapek et al., 2011; Krüttner et al., 2015; McGuire et al., 2003; Niewalda et al., 2015; Pavot et al., 2015; Qin et al., 2012; Shuai et al., 2010; Skoulakis et al., 1993; Trannoy et al., 2011; Vanover et al., 2019; Zars et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by numerous citations.

claim: Gycbeta100B has been identified as a 'memory suppressor gene' that enhances memory retention when pan-neuronally knocked down.
source: For example, the Gycbeta100B gene, which encodes a subunit of sGC, has been identified as 'memory suppressor gene' that enhances memory retention when pan-neuronally knocked down (Walkinshaw et al., 2015), but the site of its action was unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walkinshaw et al., 2015.

claim: Gycbeta100B appears to be broadly dispersed throughout KC axons, based on the observed distribution of a Gycbeta100B-EGFP fusion protein.
source: Gycbeta100B appears to be broadly dispersed throughout KC axons, based on the observed distribution of a Gycbeta100B-EGFP fusion protein (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ectopically expressing NOS in PPL1-α3 DANs that do not normally signal with NO is most easily explained if sGC is available for activation in all MB compartments.
source: Our experiments ectopically expressing NOS in PPL1-α3 DANs that do not normally signal with NO is most easily explained if sGC is available for activation in all MB compartments (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data shown in Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cultured KCs from cricket brains, cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) mediates NO-induced augmentation of a Ca2+ channel current.
source: In cultured KCs from cricket brains, cGMP-dependent protein kinase (PKG) mediates NO-induced augmentation of a Ca2+ channel current (Kosakai et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kosakai et al., 2015.

claim: The authors failed to detect expression of either of the genes encoding Drosophila PKGs (foraging and Pkg21D) in KCs in their RNA-Seq studies.
source: However, we failed to detect expression of either of the genes encoding Drosophila PKGs (foraging and Pkg21D) in KCs in our RNA-Seq studies (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde9 are expressed in KCs.
source: On the other hand, cyclic nucleotide-gated channels and the cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase Pde9 are expressed in KCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: The activity of sGC is calcium dependent.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that the activity of sGC is calcium dependent and that PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC
evidence: This claim is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC.
source: Biochemical studies have shown that the activity of sGC is calcium dependent and that PKA can enhance the NO-induced activity of sGC by phosphorylating sGC
evidence: This claim is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: sGC isolated from flies mutant for adenylate cyclase, rutabaga, show lower activity than sGC from wild-type brains.
source: sGC isolated from flies mutant for adenylate cyclase, rutabaga, show lower activity than sGC from wild-type brains (Morton et al., 2005; Shah and Hyde, 1995), suggesting crosstalk between the cAMP and cGMP pathways.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Morton et al., 2005; Shah and Hyde, 1995.

claim: The formation of a strong immediate memory interferes with and shortens the lifetimes of previously formed memories.
source: The formation of a strong immediate memory interferes with and shortens the lifetimes of previously formed memories, and reducing this interference requires a reduction in initial memory strength that can only be overcome through repeated exposure (Amit and Fusi, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amit and Fusi, 1994.

claim: Theoretical studies have argued that the tension between memory strength and longevity can be resolved by memory systems that exhibit a heterogeneity of timescales.
source: Theoretical studies have argued that this tension can be resolved by memory systems that exhibit a heterogeneity of timescales, balancing the need for both fast, labile memory and slow consolidation of reliable memories (Fusi et al., 2005; Lahiri and Ganguli, 2013; Benna and Fusi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fusi et al., 2005; Lahiri and Ganguli, 2013; Benna and Fusi, 2016.

claim: During shock conditioning, multiple DANs respond to the aversive stimulus, including PPL1-γ1pedc, PPL1-γ2α'1, PPL1-α3.
source: During shock conditioning, for example, multiple DANs respond to the aversive stimulus, including PPL1-γ1pedc, PPL1-γ2α'1, PPL1-α3 (Mao and Davis, 2009; Riemensperger et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mao and Davis, 2009; Riemensperger et al., 2005.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PPL1-γ1pedc, PPL1-γ2α'1, and PPL1-α3 individually induces negative-valence olfactory memory with distinct learning rates.
source: We have shown that optogenetic activation of these DAN cell types individually induces negative-valence olfactory memory with distinct learning rates (Aso and Rubin, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claim: The NOS-expressing PPL1-γ1pedc induces memory with the fastest learning rate in a wild-type background.
source: The NOS-expressing PPL1-γ1pedc induces memory with the fastest learning rate in a wild-type background
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and previous work cited as Aso and Rubin, 2016.

claim: Robust and stable NO-dependent effects were only observed when training was repeated 10 times.
source: Robust and stable NO-dependent effects were only observed when training was repeated 10 times (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Under repeated training, compartments with slower learning rates, such as α3, form memory traces in parallel to those formed in γ1pedc.
source: Under such repeated training, compartments with slower learning rates, such as α3, form memory traces in parallel to those formed in γ1pedc (Pai et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pai et al., 2013; Séjourné et al., 2011; Wu et al., 2017.

claim: Flies may benefit from the fast and labile memory formed in γ1pedc without suffering the potential disadvantages of shortened memory retention, as long-term memories are formed in parallel in other compartments.
source: Thus, flies may benefit from the fast and labile memory formed in γ1pedc without suffering the potential disadvantages of shortened memory retention, as long-term memories are formed in parallel in other compartments (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data and is illustrated in Figure 9B.
